content: The persistent digital divide continues to pose challenges, and many governments may not yet have the capacity to effectively regulate the use of artificial intelligence (AI). Independent scientific advice and evidence will be critical as AI evolves and is integrated into policy guidance. For AI applications in health, it is imperative that global health organizations, such as the World Health Organization (WHO), endorse only those AI technologies that have undergone rigorous testing and validation as health interventions. These technologies must also be assessed for potential risks by appropriate authorities. Global governance in this area will require adapting existing governance structures, including the policies and practices of global health agencies, WHO-issued treatment guidelines, and international agreements aimed at achieving specific health objectives, such as the elimination of HIV/AIDS by 2030. Additionally, global standards must address ethical concerns related to AI in health, including its impact on labor, data governance, privacy, ownership, and autonomous decision-making. Nongovernmental organizations (NGOs) and community groups will play a vital role in ensuring that human rights obligations and ethical principles are considered from the outset of decision-making processes. Civil society and affected communities should actively participate in the design of AI technologies. International organizations should collaborate with NGOs and affected populations to develop and mainstream guidance for governments and companies. Efforts to improve global AI governance include initiatives such as the Global Partnership on AI, established in June 2020 by the governments of Canada and France, which now includes 19 countries. This partnership aims to convene global AI experts and provide guidance on topics such as the future of work, data, and privacy. Bilateral and multilateral initiatives, such as the United Nations Secretary-General’s Roadmap for Digital Cooperation, have also been proposed to address urgent issues and coordinate follow-up actions. A multi-stakeholder high-level body could contribute to broader governance and standard-setting for AI, addressing ethical and governance challenges associated with its use in health. Global health organizations, including WHO, Gavi, the Global Fund, and Unitaid, must commit to making adherence to human rights, legal safeguards, and ethical standards a core obligation of their strategies and guidance. International agencies, such as the Council of Europe, OECD, UNESCO, and WHO, should collaborate to address the ethical challenges and opportunities of AI in health, providing coherent legal and technical support to governments.
